section_summary.extract_value: This Results section reports descriptive statistics and intercorrelations (Table 2) comparing US and non-US samples. The US sample was significantly older and had higher BMI, whereas educational level proportion was higher in the non-US sample; multigroup SEM showed acceptable-to-good fit with largely identical path coefficients across the two samples and similar standardized effects. The correlation between body appreciation and BMI was −.22 in the US sample and −.17 in the non-US sample (Table 2).
section_summary.evidence_source: "Descriptive statistics for, and intercorrelations between, all variables included in the present study are reported in Table 2." Path coefficients were nearly identical across the two samples."

section_summary.extract_value: This section reports results comparing US and non-US samples from a single study: US participants were older and had higher BMIs, while educational level proportions differed between samples. Model fit for the hypothesised (and modified) structural model was acceptable to very good across samples, standardized path coefficients were largely significant, and BMI had both a negative indirect effect on subjective happiness via body appreciation and a small positive direct effect, yielding a small negative total effect.
section_summary.evidence_source: "Participants in the US sample were significantly older, t(9,665) = 5.36, p < .001, d = .11, and had higher BMIs, t(9,665) = 8.24, p < .001, d = .17, than participants in the non-US sample."; "Fit of the hypothesised model (Fig. 1) was acceptable in the US sample, χ2 = 291.41, df = 7, p < .001, CFI = .969, TLI = .939, RMSEA = .067 [.061, .074]."; "This indirect effect had standardized coefficients of -.13 and -.11 (ps < .001), respectively, in the two samples. ... the total effect of BMI on subjective happiness was negative and had a size of only -.04 in both samples (ps < .001)."
